vignette: Mr. Thompson, 78, is an African-American librarian who has been married for more than fifty years. His life took a dramatic turn on September 15, 2016, when a terrorist attack occurred at the library where he worked. The event was a stark violation of the peaceful sanctuary he had always cherished. The sound of shattering glass and panicked screams still echoes in his mind as vividly as it did that day. Since then, Mr. Thompson has found himself navigating a world that is no longer safe or predictable. He remains deeply troubled by any hint of misbehavior, seeing it as an ominous prelude to chaos and violence. The anniversary of the attack marks a particularly difficult time for him; he spends those days in near isolation, haunted by memories that play like a continuous film loop. Even the most mundane conversations can trigger distressing recollections. A casual discussion about security measures or unexpected disasters at work sends Mr. Thompson into a state of heightened anxiety and fear. He has come to believe that any situation that might evoke feelings of happiness or hope could be shattered in an instant, just as it was during the attack. This belief has led him to avoid attending gatherings and social events, drifting instead into his own world where he can control what he thinks about. His job at the library has become increasingly challenging. Crowded places, once a familiar part of his daily routine, now trigger a flood of memories that can appear without warning. Even during quieter moments in the library, a sudden noise or movement can plunge him back into the traumatic experience. This fear has led Mr. Thompson to avoid busy sections of the library and public events, which are an integral part of his role as a librarian. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on both his professional life and personal relationships. He finds it harder to engage with colleagues and patrons, leading to strained interactions at work. His wife has noticed that he is less present in their home life, often lost in thoughts or retreating into himself when faced with potential triggers. What frightens Mr. Thompson most is the unpredictability of his memories and the constant fear that another attack could happen again. He dreads the thought of being caught off guard by a sudden reminder and feeling powerless to protect himself or others. Despite these fears, he has finally decided to seek help after realizing how much his quality of life has deteriorated over the past few years. Mr. Thompson hopes for a way to regain control of his thoughts and experiences, to find peace in places that once felt safe and familiar. He is eager to learn strategies that can help him manage his symptoms and reclaim some sense of normalcy in his daily life.
